name: Tract
parentGroup: Tract platform; separate from Quinbrook-backed Rowan
role: master developer of powered and entitled land
strategy: Creates infrastructure-ready parks and sells a development position to hyperscalers and wholesale developers. This is a land/infrastructure buyer and potential competitor to Syncranicity; it is not automatically the eventual building operator.
scale: Observed parks range from the 343-acre Morris acquisition to roughly 3,000 acres at Caldwell Valley; published ultimate loads reach gigawatts. These are precedents, not a disclosed acreage minimum. Initial contracted grid blocks and ultimate marketed capacity are different figures.

publishedRequirements.fact: Caldwell acquisitions added 1,458 contiguous acres. Its first 250 MW was contracted for Q1 2028; the much larger ultimate park includes a natural-gas/generation strategy.
Morris was acquired already zoned/entitled, with an executed ComEd Transmission Security Agreement, initial June 2028 energization target and a phased ramp through 2032.
Tract prepositions power, fiber, zoning and entitlements and engages communities before development.

inferredPreferences: Inference: prioritize assemblages where shared substations, roads and fiber can serve multiple downstream developers; a small isolated tract needs an expansion or infill role.
Inference: a credible multiyear land-control runway may matter more than an immediate cheap asking price because the infrastructure program is large.
Inference: demonstrate why a parcel improves an existing target park or opens a defensible new regional node before paying for site studies.
differentiators: Campus-level land planning and infrastructure are the product sold.
A contracted first energization block can coexist with a much larger, still phased ultimate program.
dealStructure: Documented outright acquisitions and adjacent assemblages. Willingness to acquire a third-party option or pay an assignment premium is unverified.
acquisitionSignal: January 2026 acquisitions show continuing land aggregation; they are not an open procurement request for every US parcel.
searchBrief: Search contiguous industrial tracts/assemblages in its disclosed corridors, with room for independent substation sites and heavy civil infrastructure. Seek written utility milestones and local development-agreement pathways. Do not treat Hinds-sized acreage as a substitute for campus-scale optionality.
rejectionTriggers: Inference: no credible contiguity or expansion path; parcel too small to justify shared backbone infrastructure.
Inference: community rejection or a short option that expires before the transmission program can advance.
buyerQuestions: Is the acquisition team buying new regional nodes or only adjacent expansion parcels now?
What minimum first-phase block, parcel size, control term and power security must a third-party land position have?

name: Rowan Digital Infrastructure
parentGroup: Quinbrook Infrastructure Partners; separate from Tract
strategy: Builds customer-aligned hyperscale campuses. Its origination process evaluates infrastructure corridors and regulatory conditions alongside power and expansion; an industrial site is useful only if it can be adapted to a hyperscaler specification.
scale: Published January 2025 program: multiple 200–500+ MW US campuses. These are portfolio project sizes, not a universal site minimum; utility versus critical IT basis is not consistently identified.

publishedRequirements.fact: The site-selection practice expressly screens markets, infrastructure corridors, regulation and growth patterns for hyperscale capacity and long-term expansion.
Quinbrook-backed Rowan described multiple 200–500+ MW campuses and $975M financing for its Maryland first phase in January 2025.
Current site markets powered, permitted build-to-suit capacity and reports 1.6 GW contracted power and a 6 GW pipeline; corporate totals are not parcel availability.

inferredPreferences: Inference: an expandable multi-building campus with a sponsor-ready infrastructure package is a stronger submission than a 20 MW stand-alone rural tract.
Inference: ask the customer geography first; Rowan's ability to build large loads does not mean it can create demand in an arbitrary market.
Inference: utility obligations and customer design standards need to travel with the land position; unassignable study work has limited value.
differentiators: Dedicated site-origination and economic-development roles are publicly identified.
Community agreements and customer-specific engineering are part of execution, beyond scoring generic land attributes.
dealStructure: Build-to-suit development funded with institutional project financing. Land-option assignment appetite and compensation are not publicly established.
acquisitionSignal: An active site-origination practice and large contracted pipeline support discovery outreach; no parcel-specific interest has been received.
searchBrief: Search current hyperscaler growth corridors for large industrially compatible assemblages with staged service, water infrastructure and expansion space. Ask the site origination team to name the first-phase minimum and target commercial operation year before narrowing parcels.
rejectionTriggers: Inference: insufficient campus expansion even if first-phase power is acceptable.
Inference: customer geography or design mismatch; unfinanceable utility security.
buyerQuestions: Which customer markets and first-phase sizes are still under-supplied after the existing pipeline?
Will you acquire an assignable option, or only purchase land directly after your own diligence?

name: PowerHouse Data Centers
parentGroup: Division of American Real Estate Partners (AREP); project JVs include Harrison Street and Chirisa
strategy: Real-estate-led campus development, using both powered shells and turnkey assets and partnering with land/capital owners. Distinct partner projects must not be counted as independent PowerHouse and Chirisa takeouts for the same parcel.
scale: Irving example: 50 acres and 200 MW marketed campus capacity; Reno: 49 acres and 200 MW. Project MW basis should be clarified; these are not published minimums.

publishedRequirements.fact: Irving acquisition placed a 200 MW, three-building powered-shell campus on 50 acres in a major connectivity hub, with adjacent Oncor substation access.
PowerHouse and Chirisa acquired 104 acres adjacent to an existing campus for AI-ready phased development; it offers powered-shell, build-to-suit and turnkey products.
Company press archive lists 2025 Carlisle 1.35 GW JV and January 2026 Arcola hyperscale lease announcements.

inferredPreferences: Inference: urban/near-market land can work at relatively compact acreage when multistory design and permanent power support high density.
Inference: sellers offering a credible JV or assembled adjacent land may be more useful than a thin option with no engineering access.
Inference: first-tenant underwriting and market connectivity remain decisive even if supply capacity is confirmed.
differentiators: Can build shells for other operators, so its customer can be another name in the buyer roster.
JV structure and development delivery capability distinguish it from a passive land investor.
dealStructure: Documented fee-simple land buys and project JVs. No public commitment to option assignments; validate whether it pays for origination or wants a direct seller contract.
acquisitionSignal: Continuing project/JV activity is evidenced. Individual historical delivery dates must be refreshed and are not guarantees.
searchBrief: Search 40–150+ acre industrial/technology parcels in active metros with substation room and high density building feasibility. Reno Electric Avenue is a targeted example, conditional on live utility service economics and avoiding overlap with its already controlled Reno campus.
rejectionTriggers: Inference: no hyperscale tenant demand at the proposed node.
Inference: power dates or capital obligations prevent a marketable powered-shell schedule.
buyerQuestions: Would a new parcel supplement your existing regional campus or compete with capacity you already own?
At what diligence stage would you acquire a third-party contract, and who carries utility deposits?

name: Catellus Development
parentGroup: TPG Real Estate manages Frederick project; Catellus master-development platform
role: master developer of data-center land and backbone infrastructure
regions: US redevelopment markets; new data-center acquisition mandate unverified
strategy: Master-plans, remediates and installs shared infrastructure, then sells parcels to building developers. Included as an active land-development platform, not as a direct colocation operator. Quantum Loophole has been replaced in this roster because Catellus now handles Frederick development.
scale: Frederick example: approximately 2,100 acres, 2.4 GW under development and 17.4M SF entitled according to Catellus. These are project claims, not delivered capacity or a general minimum.

publishedRequirements.fact: Catellus is master developer responsible for initial approvals and backbone water, sewer, power and telecom; Rowan and Aligned construct/operate their separate buildings.
December 2024 statement names TPG as manager and Catellus sole developer; Quantum Loophole has no active development role there.
County executive rejected the requested Development Rights and Responsibilities Agreement September 14, 2026 and extended an application pause to July 1, 2027.
Corporate project page describes a 2,100-acre campus and 40-mile fiber connection to Loudoun.

inferredPreferences: Inference: complex former industrial land with recoverable infrastructure, subdivision potential and regional interconnection advantages is more relevant than a small standalone rural tract.
Inference: public partnership, remediation allocation and long entitlement runway are unusually important for its master-development model.
Inference: no current evidence establishes that Catellus is seeking a second new data-center campus; validate mandate before prospect spending.
differentiators: Horizontal/master development rather than ownership of every data-center building.
Official county decision conflicts with the promotional impression that the proposed community agreement is already secured; use the county action for approval status.
dealStructure: Land master-development and parcel disposition evidenced. Willingness to buy options on new sites unknown.
acquisitionSignal: Active Frederick delivery confirmed; new-site procurement not confirmed.
searchBrief: Screen large brownfield assemblages near existing demand hubs only after Catellus confirms a new-site acquisition brief. Do not market new Frederick acreage as approved or unaffected by the current pause.
rejectionTriggers: Inference: no scalable backbone infrastructure or untenable remediation liabilities.
Current jurisdiction gate: unresolved Frederick application restrictions require parcel-specific review.
buyerQuestions: Are you seeking new data-center master-plan sites outside Frederick, and in what markets?
Would the platform acquire a controlled brownfield position or act only as development partner for an institutional owner?

name: Yondr
parentGroup: Yondr platform; project partners include Cerberus and JK Land Holdings
strategy: Large cloud and AI campuses in strategically connected markets. New land should compete with a substantial already controlled pipeline, not merely resemble a historical project.
scale: Observed: 40-acre Manassas acquisition for 72 MW in 2029; Loudoun 48 MW buildings with a further 240 MW adjacent pipeline; Lancaster 163-acre/550 MW plan. Basis not universally stated as IT versus facility load.

publishedRequirements.fact: August 2026 Manassas acquisition with Cerberus: 40 acres, 72 MW and planned 2029 operations; rationale emphasizes market connectivity and power timing.
Loudoun expansion is staged in 12 MW initial ready-for-service blocks within a 48 MW building and benefits from adjacent expansion land.
Texas statement places Lancaster in ERCOT Batch Zero and supports developer-funded infrastructure, water protection and predictable interconnection rules.

inferredPreferences: Inference: it can accept a multiyear delivery window when core-market power and customer demand justify it.
Inference: campus adjacency and customer continuity can outweigh cheaper remote land.
Inference: a Texas site needs clear exposure to batch/process rules and infrastructure-cost allocation, not only a MW statement.
differentiators: Institutional partner transactions demonstrate ability to structure major land acquisitions.
Phased building commissioning is distinct from ultimate campus load.
dealStructure: Land acquisition/JV and build-to-suit development evidenced; third-party option assignment policy not disclosed.
acquisitionSignal: August 2026 land purchase is a recent primary acquisition signal. It establishes activity, not interest in these prospects.
searchBrief: Search connected Northern Virginia and DFW industrial tracts with real service dates and multi-building expansion. Request geographic latency requirements and how a new site would sit alongside Lancaster/Loudoun inventory.
rejectionTriggers: Inference: remote site has no customer-specific reason to exist.
Inference: seller deadline shorter than interconnection/entitlement path; cost-shifting assumptions fail utility scrutiny.
buyerQuestions: Which North American nodes require additional land after the current pipeline?
Can a 50–75 MW first campus fit, and is a 2029+ service date acceptable for that node?

name: Related Digital
parentGroup: Related Companies; project equity partners include Blackstone
strategy: Megacampus development anchored by institutional customers and integrated energy/community arrangements. Land demand is tied to a large customer program rather than an open-ended appetite for any available acreage.
scale: Saline example: more than 1 GW planned on a 250-acre developed footprint; three 550,000 SF buildings, with surrounding conserved land. This is project evidence, not a minimum acreage/load requirement.

publishedRequirements.fact: Saline plan uses closed-loop cooling, DTE grid supply supplemented by project-financed batteries, and a large preserved open-space buffer.
Related announced financing for an Oracle/OpenAI campus, with closing subject to customary conditions in the April 2026 release.
Project outreach describes a legally limited building footprint, 75-foot minimum road setbacks and a decommissioning bond.

inferredPreferences: Inference: screen energy infrastructure and the ability to negotiate large community commitments alongside land.
Inference: industrial or rural-urban fringe assemblages need enough buffer acreage to handle local impact and siting flexibility.
Inference: an isolated 20 MW option without a relevant customer mandate is unlikely to beat its gigawatt-scale pipeline.
differentiators: Community-preservation and project-specific labor/energy commitments affect the usable acreage and economics.
A named tenant-backed program materially differentiates this model from speculative land banking.
dealStructure: Large project development with institutional equity/debt and customer commitments; willingness to pay a small originator for an unexercised option is unverified.
acquisitionSignal: 2026 financing/construction announcements evidence execution on controlled sites; no open new-site solicitation found.
searchBrief: Search major assemblages where generation/storage, workforce, customer campus architecture and community mitigation can be planned together. First validate whether a small modular first phase exists in Related's current acquisition mandate.
rejectionTriggers: Inference: no customer or partner rationale at the location.
Inference: buffer land, energy cost allocation, water policy or community agreement cannot be delivered.
buyerQuestions: Which customer-led requirements are not covered by your current campuses?
Would you consider an initial 20–50 MW land position, or is that outside the current program?

name: Chirisa Technology Parks
parentGroup: Chirisa Investments; shared project JVs with PowerHouse/Blue Owl
strategy: Combines brownfield reuse, greenfield extensions and powered-shell/turnkey delivery in established growth markets. It explicitly allows purchase or joint venture for customer build-to-suit work, an unusually useful route for a land originator to validate.
scale: Observed portfolio includes 13 MW utility power reuse in Lynnwood, 28 MW Chicago buildings and a 230-acre Richmond campus. Large project figures are utility power where the company says so; do not equate them to critical IT load.

publishedRequirements.fact: Company states it can purchase or joint venture for build-to-suit projects and co-design cooling, redundancy and density to customer needs.
Current portfolio includes adaptive reuse at Piscataway and Lynnwood alongside a large Virginia greenfield pipeline.
PowerHouse/Chirisa acquired adjacent 104-acre Meadowville land for phased AI-ready facilities; existing campus adjacency was central.

inferredPreferences: Inference: a building with reusable shell and MEP interfaces can be attractive if it removes schedule rather than adding retrofit complexity.
Inference: land adjacency to existing network/energy infrastructure is a better screening input than acreage alone.
Inference: its established land bank can displace a new raw site unless the new site wins on cost, latency or timing.
differentiators: Publicly mentions purchase/JV flexibility.
One shared Chirisa–PowerHouse JV is one correlated decision process, not two independent buyers.
dealStructure: Powered shell, turnkey, build-to-suit and JV/purchase. Assignment or fee terms require specific confirmation.
acquisitionSignal: 2025 Blue Owl JV announcements and current reserved campus phases show funded growth, while some existing pipeline already has users.
searchBrief: Search connected conversion buildings or adjacent expansion tracts in its five disclosed US clusters. NG Data Center in Chester is a targeted reuse/market-adjacency hypothesis; test actual shell suitability and whether existing commitments leave incremental demand.
rejectionTriggers: Inference: retrofit cannot deliver materially faster or cheaper than an existing reserved campus phase.
Inference: new shell cannot support desired high density, redundancy or customer architecture.
buyerQuestions: Which markets still need new land or brownfield capacity beyond current reserved phases?
What diligence package makes a landowner/JV opportunity actionable, and can the seller's option be assigned?

name: DC BLOX
parentGroup: DC BLOX platform; financial ownership not resolved in this screen
role: regional colocation, hyperscale and fiber infrastructure developer/operator
strategy: Builds data centers and the connecting dark-fiber/subsea ecosystem. For this developer, the ability to join or extend its regional network is a commercial asset, not merely a generic dual-fiber checkbox.
scale: Published hyperscale examples include 144 MW critical load on 68 Atlanta East acres, 200 MW critical load on 55 Atlanta West acres, and 40 MW Birmingham expansion. Cable-landing capacity has a different purpose from general AI IT capacity.

publishedRequirements.fact: Atlanta West specifications include N+1, liquid-cooling provisions, two meet-me rooms and dark fiber to named Atlanta hubs and Myrtle Beach.
Company expressly acquires land, secures power commitments and partners to develop hyperscale-ready sites with integrated dark fiber.
Myrtle Beach expansion used about 20 adjacent acres for additional cable systems and up to 20 MW, reflecting network-specific adjacency.

inferredPreferences: Inference: a Southeast site that adds a useful node on the Atlanta–Myrtle Beach/Palm Coast network deserves priority over a geographically unrelated cheap parcel.
Inference: require route economics, trench/ROW feasibility and named customer connectivity needs, rather than accepting a consumer broadband map.
Inference: a 20–50 MW first phase can be plausible in a regional or staged campus; it does not by itself establish demand.
differentiators: Own fiber and subsea gateway strategy creates identifiable corridor-specific preferences.
Supports both regional edge and hyperscale; determine the actual product before screening acreage.
dealStructure: Land acquisition and partnership development are documented. Option assignment purchasing is unconfirmed.
acquisitionSignal: Current corporate materials state an active land/power origination model and ongoing Southeast network expansion.
searchBrief: Search industrial parcels and reuse opportunities near its regional fiber corridors and underserved population centers. Mooresville Business Park East is a Carolinas discovery lead; first verify useful connectivity to DC BLOX's network and whether Charlotte-area demand is open.
rejectionTriggers: Inference: parcel cannot cost-effectively connect to the relevant network/customer ecosystem.
Inference: customer load is hyperscale training but the parcel only fits a small edge deployment, or vice versa.
buyerQuestions: Which fiber-route nodes currently lack enough usable data-center land?
Do you need a regional 10–40 MW campus, a cable landing node, or a 100+ MW hyperscale position?

name: TA Digital Group / TA Realty
parentGroup: TA Realty; TA Digital Group is its development arm, not an independent buyer
strategy: Builds for hyperscale tenants in Tier 1 US markets and monetizes completed stabilized assets. A prospective land option must support financeable tenant delivery and eventual asset sale, not simply a promising technical use.
scale: Published product ranges: 20–100 MW strategic infill in mature markets and 100 MW–1 GW campuses. MW basis is not specified on the solutions page. The 2026 Leesburg sale separately identifies 165 MW IT load in two completed buildings.

publishedRequirements.fact: TA expressly describes its strategy as build-to-suit hyperscale facilities in Tier 1 US markets followed by monetization on stabilization.
The Leesburg project assembled land, added utility infrastructure and provided two independent substations; platform includes Chicago and Atlanta.
TA Digital explicitly separates 20–100 MW mature-market low-latency infill from 100 MW–1 GW campuses, with build-to-suit, turnkey, powered-shell and fee-development choices.

inferredPreferences: Inference: match either a 20–100 MW low-latency infill product or a larger single-tenant/multi-building campus. Do not exclude modest acreage if it is a strong mature-market infill position.
Inference: easements and parcel geometry must preserve separate substation access and building phasing.
Inference: a small rural tract outside a Tier 1 market has low strategic relevance even with adequate MW.
Inference: underwriting must compare all-in delivered cost with alternatives already in the platform; cheap dirt is a small input to institutional asset economics.
differentiators: Stabilized sale is part of its stated business model.
Two independent substations in the disclosed flagship are a relevant design precedent, not a promise that every site requires exactly two.
dealStructure: Build-to-suit, turnkey, powered shell and fee development are published offerings. Institutional land assembly and stabilized asset sale are evidenced; a fee-development offering does not establish that TA will pay an originator an assignment fee.
acquisitionSignal: 2026 disposal release reports more than 12 owned/controlled projects and nearly 3 GW, establishing an active platform but also substantial competing inventory.
searchBrief: Run two searches: compact infill sites in mature network ecosystems for the published 20–100 MW lane, and larger expandable Tier 1 campuses for the 100 MW–1 GW lane. Specify which product a prospect serves before considering land price. Validate tenant geography and independent utility approaches.
rejectionTriggers: Inference: no Tier 1 customer requirement or no path to institutional-scale stabilization.
Inference: single critical utility corridor cannot satisfy the target tenant redundancy configuration.
buyerQuestions: What land size and MW delivery schedule fit the next tenant requirement rather than your existing campus inventory?
Can a third-party option be acquired at a defined diligence milestone or do you originate all land contracts internally?

sources.title: Published campus and infill MW ranges; delivery models

name: Sabey Data Centers
parentGroup: Sabey platform
strategy: Long-lived campuses mixing enterprise, research/HPC and hyperscale deployments. Its Pacific Northwest energy-cost proposition differs from its Austin customer/technology-corridor proposition; do not assume one nationwide site template.
scale: Austin Building B: 54 MW total power capacity, first 18 MW targeted Q3 2027, six 30,000 SF data halls. Liquid/hybrid deployments above 200 kW/rack are a design capability, not a site-selection minimum.

publishedRequirements.fact: Austin B uses a liquid-cooling-ready three-story design with phased 18 MW delivery and high-density configurations above 200 kW/rack.
Quincy markets low-cost hydropower, multiple carriers, dual campus fiber entries and an on-premises Azure on-ramp; the advertised energy rate is a site claim, not a new-parcel tariff quote.
Q1 2026 construction update says Austin B has secured utility power for the full facility and an on-site substation.

inferredPreferences: Inference: prioritize expansion-friendly industrial parcels within a demonstrated network/labor region rather than assuming cheap renewable energy alone wins.
Inference: a 10–25 MW first phase may fit its staged campus approach, but an engineering-quality heat-rejection and growth plan is necessary.
Inference: multi-story possibilities, secure equipment yards and loading access can matter more than gross acreage.
differentiators: Distinct low-cost-hydro and technology-metro products.
Proven high-density liquid-cooled operations create retrofit/design expectations that a generic warehouse may not satisfy.
dealStructure: Build-to-suit, powered shell and colocation products. New-land acquisition/assignment appetite unconfirmed.
acquisitionSignal: Existing-campus Austin growth is current; it is evidence of demand in that campus, not automatic new-market acquisition.
searchBrief: Search parcels in or close to existing Sabey regions with priced utility paths, constructible network diversity and campus growth. Ask whether the immediate need is an Austin-like staged high-density building or a Northwest low-cost-energy campus.
rejectionTriggers: Inference: seasonal cooling economics undermine the intended power-cost advantage.
Inference: no suitable regional customer/fiber ecosystem or no expansion after initial commissioning.
buyerQuestions: Where is new land needed beyond existing campuses?
What IT load, rack density and cooling configuration should the first phase support, and will you accept a powered shell?

name: Patmos
parentGroup: Patmos Hosting Inc.
strategy: Converts existing industrial/urban infrastructure into AI/HPC capacity with rapid small initial blocks. This is a better conceptual buyer for a usable powered industrial building than for an undeveloped remote farm.
scale: Kansas City example: initial 5 MW then another 7 MW; January 2026 financing announcement described a 35 MW upgrade program in a 421,112 SF former newspaper building on five acres. MW basis is not explicitly IT load.

publishedRequirements.fact: The company reported a $100M C-PACE financing for energy/HVAC/plumbing improvements at its Kansas City conversion, after staged initial deployments.
Its Technology Campus model repurposes industrial infrastructure for high-density GPU/HPC while retaining coworking/events uses.
Current development-accounting recruitment confirms a portfolio of construction/development projects and owned data-center infrastructure.

inferredPreferences: Inference: prioritize structurally usable shells with reusable electrical infrastructure and upgradeable cooling where a first phase can arrive quickly.
Inference: distinguish genuinely reusable infrastructure from expensive demolition liabilities; industrial equipment nameplates do not establish import capacity.
Inference: financing eligibility and retained ownership can matter to economics; do not assume a developer accepts a pure short-term ground lease.
differentiators: Adaptive reuse and staged capacity are central to its demonstrated execution.
Industrial shell, urban fiber and financing mechanics can be more useful than hundreds of acres.
dealStructure: Property acquisition/retrofit and long-term tenant leasing evidenced. Third-party option assignments and specific seller financing terms remain unverified.
acquisitionSignal: January 2026 financing and current development staffing establish ongoing execution; no public open acquisition checklist found.
searchBrief: Search former printing, manufacturing or enterprise-computing buildings in metros. The offered AM General plant in Mishawaka is a targeted reuse hypothesis: prove structural grid, contamination scope, cooling yards and carrier routes before claiming a fit.
rejectionTriggers: Inference: shell conversion takes longer or costs more than new construction.
Inference: stranded industrial assets cannot be reused for high-density compute or customer geography is unsupported.
buyerQuestions: What building grids, floor loading, clearance and existing electrical conditions make a conversion worth underwriting?
Would you enter a new Midwest market for a documented 10–30 MW initial phase, and can you take over an option?

name: RadiusDC
parentGroup: RadiusDC platform; Nashville development backed by Blue Owl
strategy: Targets underserved metropolitan markets with existing carrier ecosystems and complementary new campuses. For RadiusDC, network density, urban demand and expansion around an operating business are core economic inputs.
scale: Nashville precedent: roughly 12 acres for 12 MW critical power. Phoenix announced expansion targets approximately 26 MW total critical IT power; platform utility-capacity figures are larger and should not be conflated.

publishedRequirements.fact: Published platform targets supply-constrained US metropolitan markets, direct multiple-carrier access and low latency to end users/cloud/enterprise networks.
Phoenix transaction combines an existing data center, interconnection infrastructure and development rights for an additional 18 MW critical capacity from 1H 2028.
Nashville ground-up project uses a roughly 12-acre site in the urban core near multiple local and long-haul carrier routes.

inferredPreferences: Inference: a fiber-rich urban industrial parcel can outrank a much larger rural site even with identical power.
Inference: existing customers, cross-connect income and a carrier ecosystem reduce market-entry risk in an acquisition.
Inference: develop a 10–30 MW urban concept and verify the actual fiber topology rather than pitching a remote hyperscale acreage story.
differentiators: Explicit metropolitan supply-gap strategy.
Distinguishes network-dense carrier hotels from purpose-built edge campuses; prospects should be tagged accordingly.
dealStructure: Operational acquisitions with development rights and ground-up new campuses are both documented. Option assignment appetite not disclosed.
acquisitionSignal: March 2026 Phoenix acquisition agreement is a current strategic signal; the release itself says closing was expected subject to conditions, so do not infer completed closing solely from it.
searchBrief: Search urban industrial or carrier-hotel-adjacent sites in its six identified metros. Existing shell plus credible expansion can be more attractive than raw acreage. No specific currently offered site in this batch is a sufficiently direct match to justify a high-confidence forecast.
rejectionTriggers: Inference: weak carrier ecosystem despite adequate MW.
Inference: no evidence of local enterprise/edge demand or inability to create a contiguous expansion.
buyerQuestions: Which metro has unmet colocation/inference demand after current expansions?
Do you need a stabilized carrier hotel with growth rights, or a new 10–30 MW campus?

name: fifteenfortyseven Critical Systems Realty
parentGroup: 1547 platform; project capital partners vary
strategy: Builds around network aggregation and customized mission-critical requirements. Portfolio spans carrier hotels and larger powered land, so its relevant acquisition team and product must be specified before a prospect is scored.
scale: McAllen precedent: 0.5 MW existing-building addition plus a 3 MW annex. A sold Chester County land project was 100 acres with a stated 450 MW PECO commitment; these disparate products are not one standard minimum.

publishedRequirements.fact: McAllen exchange is placed in an existing cross-border US–Mexico carrier aggregation hub and expansion follows carrier and cross-connect demand.
Portfolio includes build-to-suit, powered-shell, colocation and turnkey projects; Chester County powered land is explicitly marked sold, not an available prospect.

inferredPreferences: Inference: a strategic network position or reusable carrier hotel can support a much smaller phase than a hyperscale land campus.
Inference: adjacency to established fiber routes needs measurable interconnection value, not a generic claim that fiber passes the road.
Inference: sites near its current nodes may be most actionable, but a new node requires a specific network/customer thesis.
differentiators: The value of a location may come from telecom cross-connect density rather than raw energy scale.
Proven powered-land disposition shows developer can monetize land without operating the eventual campus.
dealStructure: Custom development, operating acquisitions and powered-land sales evidenced. Contract-assignment versus direct-title acquisition policy unknown.
acquisitionSignal: Current McAllen exchange/annex activity demonstrates network-led growth. It does not establish an active 450 MW land-buying mandate everywhere.
searchBrief: Search carrier-hotel expansions, cross-border gateway nodes and industrial reuse in existing metros. Mishawaka is near its disclosed South Bend market but actual route diversity and incremental demand need verification; geographic proximity alone is not enough.
rejectionTriggers: Inference: no carrier or customer reason for the node.
Inference: offered site is actually an investment sale with no vacant redevelopment capacity or lacks useful network access rights.
buyerQuestions: Which locations need an additional building rather than space inside an existing carrier hotel?
What makes a third-party land position valuable to your powered-shell versus interconnection team?

name: Novva Data Centers
parentGroup: Novva; CIM Group investment partner
strategy: Purpose-built Western campuses with water-free cooling and a high-density AI proposition. Land matching needs to consider climate, dry heat rejection, fiber and campus efficiency together; abundant water is not its defining differentiator.
scale: Mesa precedent: 160 acres, marketed 300 MW campus, first phase 96 MW critical IT load. Reno precedent: 20 acres with six 10 MW halls and a 100 MW substation. Substation rating is not the same as IT capacity or a procurement threshold.

publishedRequirements.fact: Mesa design uses water-free cooling, direct-to-chip readiness, east/west-oriented halls, rain capture and public paths; land was acquired through state auction.
Salt Lake rationale names low-cost power, low latency, long-haul fiber, international airport proximity, equipment-tax economics and cold-desert climate.
Reno specifications describe air-cooled chillers, fiber-route crossroads and a multi-hall format at Tahoe Reno Industrial Center.

inferredPreferences: Inference: avoid automatically rejecting dry regions for cooling water, but validate peak ambient-temperature derating and energy cost.
Inference: a Western industrial park parcel with established fiber and airport/workforce access is a stronger match than equally cheap unserviced desert acreage.
Inference: compare a new parcel with Novva's already controlled regional capacity; expansion headroom alone does not prove new-site need.
differentiators: Water-free architecture changes the screening priority from bulk evaporative supply to heat-rejection economics.
Architectural orientation, outdoor plant area and community integration affect usable land.
dealStructure: Land acquisition and institutional campus financing documented; assignment purchase terms unknown.
acquisitionSignal: Ongoing Mesa/Utah/Reno development confirms Western strategy, but published first-phase dates are project targets requiring refresh.
searchBrief: Search entitled Western industrial parcels. The 75-acre Electric Avenue listing inside TRIC is a precise regional/park match for discovery; verify NV Energy delivery, cooling setbacks and whether its existing Reno campus already meets demand.
rejectionTriggers: Inference: summer cooling derating or tariff cost defeats the advertised efficiency proposition.
Inference: no incremental tenant rationale beyond an existing regional campus.
buyerQuestions: Which Western regions need new land now, and what gap remains after current campuses?
Would TRIC expansion land be useful, and what minimum first-phase IT load and delivery date matter?

sources.title: CIM Novva expansion financing and criteria

name: CleanArc Data Centers
parentGroup: CleanArc platform; Crow Holdings land partnership in Dallas
strategy: Its published site strategy is Tier 1 Adjacent: achieve hub-quality connectivity without every core-market constraint. This is an unusually specific filter that should be tested using network engineering rather than map distance.
scale: Dallas example: 40 acres, 245 MW marketed ultimate campus, 70 MW first building planned late 2027. Figure basis should be clarified before treating it as critical IT load.

publishedRequirements.fact: CleanArc defines target Tier 1 Adjacent locations as typically within approximately two milliseconds round-trip latency of a major carrier hotel or internet exchange.
Dallas project uses Crow Holdings-owned urban infill land near Infomart/2323 Bryan, with CleanArc leading technical design, substation construction and tenant engagement.
Published locations include Virginia/Dallas, Austin and southern Dallas work in progress, and Chicago/Atlanta future-growth labels.

inferredPreferences: Inference: route length, optical equipment and actual RTT to the named hub should be a pre-screen gate; straight-line miles are insufficient.
Inference: a landowner partnership can be viable without the developer initially buying fee title.
Inference: compact, highly connected sites may compete well with large campuses when density and power support the use.
differentiators: Explicit ~2 ms RTT target goes beyond a generic fiber requirement.
Development-and-leasing partnership on another owner's land is documented.
dealStructure: Landowner/developer partnership evidenced. Option assignment, ground lease and fee schedule are transaction-specific and unverified.
acquisitionSignal: February 2026 central-Dallas appointment and published future-growth markets are useful current search signals, not an acquisition guarantee.
searchBrief: Start from Infomart, 2323 Bryan, Atlanta interconnection hubs or the relevant Virginia hub and trace feasible low-latency routes outward. Screen land only inside a defensible network envelope, then test scalable service and land-control economics.
rejectionTriggers: Published strategy mismatch: cannot plausibly meet the relevant hub RTT.
Inference: property is cheap because fiber build and route rights consume the schedule/cost advantage.
buyerQuestions: Which carrier hotel or IX and what measured RTT define the requirement for the next site?
Would you partner with a landowner through an assignable option, and what power milestone must be reached first?

name: AVAIO Digital Partners
parentGroup: AVAIO Digital private platform
role: hyperscale/AI developer/operator integrating grid and on-site energy
strategy: Seeks integrated campuses where grid service, possible behind-the-meter generation, network routes and community support can be combined. A natural-gas pipeline is relevant only after deliverability, firm gas service and air-permit economics are established.
scale: Current portfolio markets first phases of 50–150 MW baseload capacity. Little Rock source conflict: January announcement described 760 acres/Q2 2027 power, whereas current project page says 296 acres and Q4 2027 initial grid capacity. Treat scope/timeline as unresolved rather than choosing the optimistic version.

publishedRequirements.fact: January Little Rock selection rationale named long-haul/regional routes to Dallas/Atlanta/Memphis, rapid Entergy power, on-site gas infrastructure and room for campus-plus-generation.
Current Leo page describes four non-single-point-of-failure fiber entrances, existing water/sewer, approved site plan and executed Entergy ESA; figures and dates differ from the launch release.
Company offers turnkey, build-to-suit and powered shell with potential thermal/renewable behind-the-meter capacity.

inferredPreferences: Inference: reserve acreage and permitting room for generation, gas lateral, cooling and electrical yards, not just data halls.
Inference: require signed service assumptions, phased ramp and tariff economics instead of counting future generation as immediately available power.
Inference: named interregional fiber markets and supportive authorities are useful initial filters.
differentiators: Grid plus behind-the-meter flexibility is central to the offering.
Contradictory public project scope demonstrates why one announcement cannot be treated as a complete buyer specification.
dealStructure: Campus development with flexible turnkey/powered-shell products. New-site option assignment policy unverified.
acquisitionSignal: Current multi-campus pipeline is active; capacity marketing is not evidence of additional land procurement demand.
searchBrief: Search large industrial parcels in utility-friendly secondary metros with actual gas and fiber service paths. Ask whether new 20–50 MW opportunities are welcome or whether origination now targets larger initial blocks; the initial tranche matters more than ultimate marketing capacity.
rejectionTriggers: Inference: no lawful/economic on-site generation path where the schedule depends on it.
Inference: late grid delivery cannot be bridged at customer-acceptable cost or environmental performance.
buyerQuestions: What minimum initial baseload and ultimate grid/BTM split should a new site support?
Which published Leo acreage and power dates reflect the current scope, and which assumptions transfer to new sites?

name: Verrus
parentGroup: Sidewalk Infrastructure Partners-backed; Alphabet is an investor in SIP, not an independent site-specific takeout
role: greenfield hyperscale developer with integrated battery-energy management
regions: United States; specific current acquisition markets not disclosed in reviewed primary sources
strategy: Builds grid-responsive campuses using on-site batteries and proprietary control systems to combine high-availability computing with flexible AI workloads. The actual utility tariff, grid-service rules and workload mix matter unusually much to its site thesis.
scale: No defensible public minimum acreage or first-phase MW found. Corporate materials advertise availability up to 99.999% where required; that is a service-design claim, not a universal load-curtailment allowance.

publishedRequirements.fact: Company describes balancing grid, carbon and compute requirements, including flexible/batched AI workloads and high-availability service.
Its primary recruitment material identifies greenfield hyperscale construction with large-scale BESS, grid services and capitalized turnkey facilities.
Community role description requires early engagement and portfolio-level tracking of sentiment, permitting and economic effects.

inferredPreferences: Inference: target greenfield industrial land with room and permitting pathways for BESS and multiple electrical operating modes.
Inference: a utility willing to contract for responsive load may be a better partner than one offering a nominally cheaper inflexible service.
Inference: customer tolerance for variable uptime cannot be assumed; the mix must be specified in the buyer brief.
differentiators: Workload-aware energy operation makes tariff and controllability central, beyond bulk MW.
No disclosed current geography/minimum means parcel-fit confidence must remain low until buyer discovery.
dealStructure: Developer capitalizes turnkey campuses; land acquisition, JV and assignment terms not public.
acquisitionSignal: Current engineering/community hiring and active platform support continued development. No parcel acquisition mandate was verified.
searchBrief: Obtain its active utility/market brief first. Then search BESS-compatible industrial land where dispatch, interconnection, fire setbacks, emissions and customer service obligations can be engineered together. Avoid manufacturing a site preference from office location.
rejectionTriggers: Inference: utility rules prevent the intended flexible-load/BESS operation.
Inference: no safe/permitable storage layout or customer load cannot tolerate the chosen flexibility.
buyerQuestions: Which utilities and markets currently value your responsive-load model?
What acreage, BESS duration, first-phase MW and customer SLA must a new site accommodate?

name: Giga Energy
parentGroup: Giga Energy; distinct from older GIGA Data Centers brand
role: AI infrastructure manufacturer and site developer/operator
regions: PJM; exact acquisition utility territories require confirmation
strategy: Combines utility origination, land, in-house electrical/modular equipment, construction and operations. It develops both owned sites and customer sites; the opportunity can be a commercial partnership rather than a simple land sale.
scale: Company reports 175 MW developed/operating across 15 sites and 500+ MW pipeline. Modular product example uses 1.4 MW compute pods; neither portfolio totals nor pod size establish a minimum site demand.

publishedRequirements.fact: Public site-development model targets underused power and dormant industrial/commercial assets, with controllable load and in-house engineering/construction.
Turnkey description specifies utility origination, site permitting, grading/drainage, substation/interconnection and factory-tested pod deployment.
Company states it builds on customer land or its own with flexible deal structures and high-density colocation.

inferredPreferences: Inference: smaller staged industrial power positions can be more relevant here than to a gigawatt-only master developer.
Inference: compatibility with repeatable module pads, access and cooling is a useful civil screen.
Inference: if a utility partnership already supplies the same power opportunity, merely controlling adjacent land may not earn a premium.
differentiators: Manufacturing control can remove equipment bottlenecks but cannot remove utility, land or permit constraints.
Developer explicitly describes both customer-owned and self-owned site models.
dealStructure: Build-to-suit, own-site colocation and customer-site construction are documented. Distinguish being an equipment customer from being a land seller; confirm purchase/JV/assignment appetite.
acquisitionSignal: Current primary site identifies a live site-origination/development practice. Replaces GIGA Data Centers in the roster to avoid relying on a stale, different brand.
searchBrief: Search dormant industrial/commercial sites with realistic staged utility service, pad-ready geometry and room for modular expansion. A 10–30 MW pilot can be a discovery hypothesis, not a published Giga acquisition minimum.
rejectionTriggers: Inference: unfirm power/curtailment terms conflict with the intended AI customer SLA.
Inference: no land margin remains after Giga can source an equivalent utility-backed site directly.
buyerQuestions: Which utilities have surplus/underused service positions you need land around?
Would you buy an option, partner with the landowner, or only provide paid construction on a customer's site?

name: TECfusions
parentGroup: TECfusions platform
strategy: Adaptive industrial reuse with direct liquid cooling and staged grid-to-behind-the-meter energy strategies. Buyer fit depends on rapid practical reuse and funded customer deployment, not simply a large future MW headline.
scale: January 2026 company report described 10 MW additions in Tucson and Pennsylvania; prior Tucson phase 14.4 MW. San Antonio flyer describes 111 acres and 20 MW initial/300 MW future. These are company marketing claims, not independently verified deliverability.

publishedRequirements.fact: January 2026 company report describes 20 MW of TensorWave expansion split between Tucson and Keystone, direct liquid cooling, and a Pennsylvania grid-to-BTM phasing strategy.
San Antonio product flyer describes adaptive reuse and a target contract-to-deployment period below six months.
October 2024 TensorWave announcement links customer capacity commitments to adaptive-reuse delivery across the portfolio.

inferredPreferences: Inference: seek industrial buildings with reusable structure, electrical rooms and cooling space where permits/fit-out can actually be accelerated.
Inference: on-site generation needs its own gas, air, noise and reliability proof; existing industrial zoning is not blanket authorization.
Inference: a smaller near-term block can matter if it serves an identified cluster/customer and leaves room for expansion.
differentiators: Adaptive reuse and direct-liquid-cooled AI are core to the model.
Separate immediate deployment from aspirational gigawatt BTM growth.
dealStructure: Owns/develops reused campuses and leases AI infrastructure; option/PSA assignment policy unconfirmed.
acquisitionSignal: Current company expansion report is a customer-specific signal. Its category webpage was searchable but returned 404 on direct opening, so use the underlying company PDFs and request current milestones before relying on dates.
searchBrief: Screen former factories and industrial campuses, including the marketed AM General plant at Mishawaka. Require a structural/civil conversion test, contamination allocation, useful fiber and a written utility response; a building's prior peak usage does not prove today's capacity.
rejectionTriggers: Inference: retrofit cannot meet density, cooling or speed objectives.
Inference: BTM plan substitutes speculative generation for a contracted service path.
buyerQuestions: Which industrial shell features let you deliver a 10–25 MW first phase within customer timing?
Would you consider Mishawaka or other Midwest reuse, and what customer/energy prerequisites must be present?

sources.title: TensorWave 20 MW expansion report; direct page returned 404

name: Edged US
parentGroup: Endeavour platform
strategy: Builds high-density facilities for regional inference and hyperscale customers using waterless cooling. Its public siting framework connects grid capacity, actual network pathways, transport, real-estate conditions and community alignment from the outset.
scale: Observed US campus sizes include 13 MW Des Moines, 24 MW Dallas/Columbus, 26 MW Kansas City, 36 MW Phoenix and 169 MW Atlanta. Current examples demonstrate more than a single hyperscale minimum.

publishedRequirements.fact: Published site-selection process evaluates scalable power, fiber pathways, transportation, real-estate conditions, community alignment, permitting, constructability and future scale.
Atlanta third building is 42 MW critical capacity and designed for 400+ kW/rack liquid or 120+ kW/rack air cooling; this is facility design, not a site minimum.
Atlanta campus specifications include two meet-me rooms, multiple providers and four diverse entrances, with waterless cooling.
September 2026 release reports topping out two buildings of its 200 MW Council Bluffs campus; this is already controlled competing inventory, not land available for origination.

inferredPreferences: Inference: a near-metro 20–40 MW site can be a more relevant first conversation than a remote gigawatt promise.
Inference: carrier routes serving regional users and a practical dry-cooling equipment layout are key differentiators.
Inference: the same city is not enough; compare the new parcel against its owned/under-construction campus and prove incremental customer need.
differentiators: Published geospatial site-selection workflow is unusually explicit.
Waterless heat rejection changes the land/cooling screen, while extreme rack density raises equipment-yard and electrical design demands.
dealStructure: Develops and operates facilities, including reused industrial land; landowner/JV/option acquisition route not publicly specified.
acquisitionSignal: 2026 Atlanta construction and current national portfolio establish activity. Existing facilities and pipeline are comparables, not available land for Syncranicity to option.
searchBrief: Search industrially compatible metropolitan sites with 20–50 MW staged expansion, network routes and cooling yards. Council Bluffs 121-acre broker listing is a regional-match lead; flood exposure near Lake Manawa and local fiber/service details remain gating unknowns.
rejectionTriggers: Inference: regional latency/customer thesis is absent.
Inference: claimed zero cooling-water use is incorrectly taken to mean no fire/domestic water or no heat/noise impacts.
buyerQuestions: Which metros require land beyond your current campus pipeline?
What first-phase critical MW, density, network endpoints and expansion margin should a new parcel be designed around?

sources.title: Council Bluffs 200 MW campus topping out
